status_key.qualified: Allowed only with the stated qualifier.
status_key.blocked: Not supported: the Verifier blocks it.

global_rules.rule: Every percentage names its baseline: vs his match average, vs his peak, vs the first 15 min, or of a typical professional's reserve.
Every fatigue statement uses estimate language (likely, our estimate, the data suggest) or the typical-professional wording.
Context check before 'tired' or 'fatigue': ball in play, score, start of a half, first-half load, role, just substituted on, just lost or won the ball.
No claims about an individual's physiology (lactate, glycogen); only estimates from movement.
Compare phases per minute of that phase, never as raw totals.
The battery and the low-battery chance describe the running, relative to a typical professional, never the player's own state.
Plain English on screen: no field names or code identifiers (times_exposed_so_far, vs_opponent).

claims.pattern: After his hardest minutes, high-speed running drops for a few minutes and then recovers
claims.wording: After a player's hardest 5 minutes, high-speed running in the next minute is typically about 40% below their match average. It comes back over about 5 minutes.

claims.pattern: Longer spells need longer recovery; sprinting recovers slowest
claims.wording: Short bursts are shaken off in a minute or two. A five-minute spell takes about five minutes, and sprinting takes longer.

claims.pattern: After a peak, players do less covering and recovery running out of possession (EPL)
claims.wording: In the Premier League, players make about a third fewer high-speed recovery runs right after their hardest minutes of the match than they normally do.

claims.pattern: Transitions, especially just after losing the ball, are the most demanding moments
claims.wording: Losing the ball forces the hardest running of the game. This is where tired legs get exposed.

claims.pattern: After a peak, runs get shorter; carries and receptions get slower
claims.wording: His runs after that spell are shorter, and he's receiving the ball at lower speed.

claims.pattern: Fresh substitutes cover more high-intensity distance per minute
claims.wording: Fresh legs: substitutes typically do 15–25% more high-intensity running per minute than players who started.

claims.pattern: Toward the end, less moderate-to-high-speed running and fewer accelerations, longer gaps between efforts
claims.wording: In the last 15 minutes, players typically do about a fifth less hard running than at kick-off, with longer breaks between efforts.

claims.pattern: Total distance recovers faster than high-speed running
claims.wording: He's still moving, but the high-speed runs aren't there yet.

claims.pattern: Temporary fatigue is not caused by lactic acid
claims.wording: It isn't 'lactic acid'. Scientists think it's a short-lived disturbance in the muscle's salt balance, which clears in minutes.

claims.pattern: Both teams' running rises and falls together
claims.wording: When one side raises the tempo, the other has to match it: in the Premier League the two teams' running totals move closely together.

claims.pattern: Teams run harder per minute without the ball than with it
claims.wording: Without the ball, Premier League players typically cover about 10% more ground per minute than when they have it.

claims.pattern: Recovery starts fast: part of short-term capacity returns within 30 s (lab, cycling)
claims.wording: In lab tests, about a fifth of the short-term reserve returns in the first 30 seconds of easy recovery.

claims.pattern: He's slower now (top speed)
claims.qualifier: Only for repeated efforts or after a peak; never 'he's lost his pace'.
claims.wording: His last few sprints were a bit slower than earlier ones.

claims.pattern: Battery / D′ balance and the typical-pro chance
claims.qualifier: Relative to a typical professional only (decision 14), with the band; the chance quoted with its measured calibration.
claims.wording: He has done running that would leave a typical professional at about 40% of their short-term reserve.

claims.pattern: Equivalent distance
claims.wording: About 11 km, an effort roughly like 13 km of steady running (model estimate).

claims.pattern: Drop in running due to fatigue vs tactics
claims.wording: His running dropped while his team sat on a 3–0 lead, so this may be tactical rather than fatigue.

claims.pattern: Pass, shot or touch volume falls after peaks or late
claims.qualifier: Only together with ball in play.
claims.wording: Fewer touches, partly because the ball was out of play more.

claims.pattern: Second-half drop
claims.wording: Players who ran hardest before the break usually do a bit less after it.

claims.pattern: Kicking / pass speed and shot precision drop
claims.qualifier: Lab only, analyst mode, never applied to a specific pass.
claims.wording: In lab tests, tired players strike the ball a little slower and less precisely.

claims.pattern: Space lost because he's tired (pitch control)
claims.wording: Model view: if he were fresh, we estimate he'd control a bit more of this area.

claims.pattern: Extreme spells → central midfielders lose the ball more
claims.qualifier: Analyst mode only, a weak association in one league.
claims.wording: In one league, central midfielders lost the ball a little more in their most extreme spells (a weak association).

claims.pattern: Acceleration–speed profile shows fatigue
claims.qualifier: Analyst mode, post-match, half vs half, low confidence.
claims.wording: Post-match, low confidence: his acceleration profile in the second half sits a little below the first.

claims.pattern: Teams that sprint more finish higher
claims.qualifier: A weak link, not a recipe.
claims.wording: Higher-placed teams tend to sprint a little more; it's a weak link, not a recipe.

claims.pattern: Pressing harder goes with success
claims.wording: Successful teams tend to work harder without the ball than with it.

claims.pattern: His battery is empty / he's exhausted
claims.qualifier: Only relative: lowest point of his match, lower than his teammates.
claims.wording: This is the lowest point of his match so far, by our estimate.

claims.pattern: Players pace themselves
claims.qualifier: Analyst mode, general only; never about one player's choices.
claims.wording: When players can't choose their pace, as in lab simulations, running drops much earlier. In matches they spread their effort.

claims.pattern: Misplaced the pass because he was tired
claims.alternative: He'd just finished a hard spell. In general, passing accuracy holds up under fatigue.

claims.pattern: Bad decision / lost concentration because tired
Missed the shot because tired
He can't accelerate any more right after a peak
claims.alternative: He's still making short bursts, but fewer long high-speed runs.

claims.pattern: Any % without a baseline, or a vs-the-peak drop (−93%, −77%) presented as below normal
His lactic acid / lactate is high
Tired from Wednesday's match
Heart-rate claims (his heart rate is 180)
Tired forwards lose the most space
Exact numbers for one player's physiology presented as measured, including a critical speed from this match
They won because they ran more / outran them, so they won
claims.alternative: Both teams ran a similar amount; the difference was in what they did with it.

claims.pattern: They ran more with the ball, so they played better
Comparing a player's acceleration count with a published number
claims.alternative: Compare only with his own earlier periods.

claims.pattern: He is tired / he is at 40% / his battery is at 40% / he is running on empty
claims.alternative: He has done running that would leave a typical professional at about 40% of their reserve (claim 11).

claims.pattern: He ran more, so he's fitter / he ran less, so he's unfit
claims.alternative: Describe the running only: he covered 11.4 km, the most on his team.

claims.pattern: Team X is more tired / fresher / fitter than team Y (team-level fatigue or fitness)
claims.alternative: Albion have done more high-speed running per ball-in-play minute than Ravensholt in the last 15 minutes (measured).

claims.pattern: Top speed hardly drops over a match
claims.wording: Top speed hardly drops over a match: in the Premier League, players' fastest runs late on are almost as fast as their fastest early on.

claims.pattern: Runs near a player's real top speed are rare in matches
claims.wording: Flat-out running is rare: Premier League players cover only about 20–30 m a match above 85% of their season top speed.

claims.pattern: Effort or intent read from speed: he didn't try, gave up, jogged back, should have sprinted, lacked desire
claims.alternative: He ran back at 5.8 m/s (21 km/h), 70% of his top speed today, and the gap grew from 4 to 9 m.

claims.pattern: Pressing or closing down read from positions (what a run or a team meant to do)
claims.alternative: Without the ball, with it in the opponents' third, Albion did 146 m of high-speed running per minute of that situation (measured).
